chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from some of our companions, from Sufyan ibn al-Sim't, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
You prostrate the two prostrations of forgetfulness for every addition that comes to you or omission, and whoever leaves a prostration has diminished (the prayer).

And this narration does not negate the one we presented earlier, which is the narration of Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) when he mentioned the ruling for one who forgot a prostration and did not mention it except after bowing, he said: He fulfills it after the prayer, and there is no forgetfulness upon him.

Because his saying (peace be upon him) 'and there is no forgetfulness upon him' means that his ruling is not the ruling of those who are forgetful, but rather the ruling of those who cut short, because when he remembers what was missed and fulfills it, nothing remains upon him of which he is doubtful, so he exits the boundary of forgetfulness.

As for what the narration of al-Halabi included, that if he doubts in one prostration or two, he adds one prostration to it and there are not two prostrations of forgetfulness upon him, then this is restricted to one for whom this is the ruling.

And we have made the two prostrations of forgetfulness obligatory for one who knows after bowing that he left a prostration, for he fulfills it after the salutation and prostrates the two prostrations of forgetfulness.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on prostrations of forgetfulness when a prostration is missed and remembered after bowing?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the Shia jurisprudential distinction between simple omission (*qada'*) and technical forgetfulness (*sahw*) by resolving apparent contradictions in reports from Imam al-Sadiq. It establishes that while any addition or omission generally triggers the two prostrations of forgetfulness, a specific case of remembering a missed prostration after *ruku'* is treated as a simple debt rather than a defect of attention, thereby exempting the worshipper from the additional *sajdat al-sahw*. This nuanced ruling highlights the Shia emphasis on precise intention and the specific timing of error within the prayer structure.
